item.title: How to Watch Ayra Starr’s NFL Halftime Performance: Kick-Off Time and Where to Stream
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Ayra Starr makes history as the first African artiste to headline an NFL international halftime show at London’s Tottenham Hotspur Stadium during the Philadelphia Eagles vs Jacksonville Jaguars game on October 11, 2026.

The post How to Watch Ayra Starr’s NFL Halftime Performance: Kick-Off Time and Where to Stream appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Ayra Starr at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium ahead of her historic NFL halftime show performance in London.

Ayra Starr is taking Afrobeats to the football field, and this time, we’re talking American football! The Nigerian superstar is set to make history as the first African artiste to headline an NFL international halftime show when she performs at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Sunday, 11 October 2026. And with the Philadelphia Eagles facing the Jacksonville Jaguars, football fans will have a little extra entertainment to look forward to during the break.

For Ayra, whose music has travelled from Nigeria to audiences around the world, this is another exciting addition to her growing list of international performances. This time, she’ll be introducing even more sports fans to her music, with songs from her Starrgirl project making their way to one of the NFL’s biggest international platforms.

And what can fans expect to hear? Well, we’re hoping some of our favourites make the setlist. Perhaps “Hot Body” and “Tornado”, or even “Heaven Baby”, her collaboration with ZAYN. Nothing has been confirmed about the songs she’ll perform, but we’re already curious to see what she has planned for the halftime show.

Ayra Starr speaking at the NFL London Games press conference ahead of her performance.

If you’re planning to watch from Nigeria, here’s what you need to know. The Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars game is scheduled to kick off at 2:30 PM British Summer Time (BST), which is 2:30 PM West Africa Time (WAT). In the UK, viewers can catch the game on ITV1 and Sky Sports NFL, while fans in Nigeria and other supported regions can watch through DAZN’s NFL Game Pass. Viewers in the United States can tune in on FOX. The halftime performance will take place during the match, so keep an eye on the game if you don’t want to miss Ayra’s set.

From performing her songs on music stages to preparing for an NFL halftime show in London, Ayra Starr keeps finding new audiences for her music. And for Nigerian fans watching from home, there’s something particularly exciting about seeing one of our own take the stage at an international sporting event of this scale.

item.content:encoded:
Ejovwoke Obas Olikuntuyi delivers a powerful performance as Ejiro in Her Daughters’ Mother

Nollywood is having an incredible global moment, and we couldn’t be prouder to cheer on our home-grown talents as they take their stories to the world. Filmmaker Chinazaekpere Chukwu is making her feature directorial debut with Her Daughters’ Mother, and the poignant Nigerian drama has been officially selected to screen at Film Africa 2026.

Scheduled for an October 28 screening at the newly launched EbonyLife Place London, the 110-minute feature explores womanhood, sacrifice, and the enduring bond between mothers and daughters.

Speaking on the emotional backbone of the project, Chinazaekpere Chukwu shared:

It’s intended to feel like a juxtaposition of ‘The Joys of Motherhood‘ by Buchi Emecheta and ‘Stay With Me’ by Ayọ̀bámi Adébáyọ̀. It reaches deep into the rights of women, how their lives are decided for them until the end, first by their families/spouses and finally by their kids.

Her Daughters’ Mother highlights the quiet resilience and domestic weight carried by women across generations.

Set against the rich cultural backdrop of Benin and filmed early this year in English, Pidgin, Urhobo, and Bini, the story follows 33-year-old Ejiro (played by Ejovwoke Obas Olikuntuyi). After being married off at the tender age of 16, Ejiro returns home in her thirties as a widowed mother of two daughters, determined to secure a brighter future for them.

Faced with limited options, she enters a second marriage with Osato (Philip Asaya), a lorry driver who promises security and education for her girls in exchange for a male heir. However, when Ejiro struggles to fulfill his demands, Osato’s entitlement turns her life into a nightmare, leaving her longing for the freedom she last felt as a child. Meanwhile, her eldest daughter Ejaita (Osas Okonyon), a bright 16-year-old dreaming of becoming a doctor, struggles against her mother’s overprotectiveness, unaware of the immense sacrifices being made on her behalf.

Osas Okonyon stars as Ejaita, a bright teenager whose ambitious dreams clash with her mother’s protective sacrifices.

The film boasts an exceptional cast, including Najite Dede and Adeoluwa Akintoba. Behind the scenes, Chukwu—who wrote the screenplay alongside Sunday Melvin Iwinosa from a story by Efosa Ogbomo—collaborated with cinematographer Yinka Adegoke, executive producer and co-producer Efosa Ogbomo, and story consultant and editor Joshua Tsotso.

Adeoluwa Akintoba in a scene from Her Daughters’ Mother, exploring youth and ambition.

Chukwu’s transition to feature filmmaking follows her award-winning streak at the EbonyLife Creative Academy, where she graduated with the Best Director award for A Psalm for Abigail, as well as her standout short film Ti e Nbo, which screened in the Shorts category at AFRIFF in 2023. Produced by One Child Grace Studio in association with C.A.N.O Productions, Uncut Gem Productions, and Nka Pictures, Her Daughters’ Mother promises to deliver a deeply moving, authentic Nigerian narrative that resonates across borders.

item.content:encoded:
BBNaija Season 11 finalists Sheba, Aikou, and winner Temi Nkem reflect on living boldly during their Guinness post-eviction sit-down.

As intense as Big Brother Naija can get, nothing quite compares to the tension of finale night! Who will make it into the final five? Who will be among the last three standing? And when Ebuka Obi–Uchendu finally announces the first runner-up, whose name will he call as the winner? Now, imagine being one of the housemates standing on that stage, waiting to hear your name. The suspense alone!

But making it that far is a story of its own. The final ten housemates had spent weeks navigating friendships, disagreements, nominations, wagers and all the surprises Biggie had waiting for them. Getting into the Top 10 meant they had played the game boldly, made decisions along the way and found ways to keep going, even when things didn’t work out as planned.

And when the season finally wrapped up, we had a few questions for the last five standing. With Guinness, a brand that celebrates boldness and authenticity, powering our BBNaija Season 11 finale post-eviction interviews, we sat down with winner Temi Nkem and fellow finalists Aikou, Sheba, Tram and Bluethopia to talk about their time in Biggie’s house, the choices they made, the courage it took to stay true to themselves and what comes next.

 

View this post on Instagram

Of course, we wanted to know how they managed to remain grounded while living with a houseful of distinct personalities under 24/7 camera surveillance. There were friendships to navigate, difficult decisions to make and times when speaking up or standing your ground took courage. So, what did living boldly look like for each of them?

For Temi Nkem, the conversation explored the instincts and decisions that helped her navigate the competition all the way to the winning spot. Aikou, Sheba, Tram and Bluethopia also reflected on their individual journeys, how they approached the game and what they learnt about themselves along the way.

And now that the cameras are off and life outside Biggie’s house has begun, what’s next? The finalists shared their plans for the future, the opportunities they’re looking forward to and how they hope to carry that same boldness into their next chapters.

Powered by Guinness, these conversations gave us another chance to hear from the housemates after the competition, this time with the pressure of nominations and evictions behind them. If there is one thing about life in Biggie’s house, it is that there is always something going on. Between the housemates’ conversations, their daily routines, the strategies and the tasks that kept them on their toes, BBNaija Season 11 had no shortage of activity. And through it all, Checkers Custard was right there, serving the housemates creamy custard throughout the show. Because even when you are busy navigating life with 23 other people, there is always room for a comforting bowl of custard!

From breakfast before the day’s activities to kitchen catch-ups with fellow housemates, Checkers Custard was part of the everyday experience inside the house. Those kitchen visits were also a chance to catch up, share a laugh and take a breather before the next task or surprise from Biggie. With so much happening under one roof, having something creamy to enjoy was a welcome addition to the routine.

And speaking of tasks, Checkers Custard had something special in store for the housemates, too. The Checkers Custard Task called for mental agility, physical endurance and teamwork, giving the housemates a chance to put their skills to the test. With Head of House Tram stepping in as Game Master, the house was split into two teams: Team Creamy and Team Tasty. Now, it was time to see which side could pull together and claim the win.

item.content:encoded:
Funmilola Sanya and Dorcas Anya head to Kampala for the Africa Destination Celebrations Conference & Expo (ADCCE 2026) to cover the latest in African celebration tourism for BellaNaija.

Hi BNers, we’re heading to Uganda! From October 12th to 17th, 2026, BellaNaija’s Funmilola Sanya and Dorcas Anya will be in Kampala for the Africa Destination Celebrations Conference & Expo (ADCCE 2026).

With the theme “Africa Unveils Events in the Wild,” ADCCE 2026 brings together wedding and event professionals, tourism stakeholders, hospitality executives, creatives, cultural curators, and industry leaders to explore Africa’s potential as the Celebration Capital of the World.

The conference and expo will take place on 12th and 13th October 2026 at the Speke Resort Munyonyo Convention Centre in Kampala, Uganda, followed by destination experiences and familiarisation tours from October 14th to 17th.

The gathering aims to showcase Africa’s rich cultural heritage, breathtaking landscapes, unique destinations, and world-class hospitality while creating opportunities for collaboration, investment, and growth across the continent’s celebration and tourism industries.

Despite Africa’s incredible destinations and creative talent, the continent remains underrepresented in the global destination wedding and celebration tourism market. ADCCE seeks to change that narrative by connecting African destinations and businesses with international industry professionals and creating greater visibility for the continent’s offerings.

For BellaNaija, this is an opportunity to experience Uganda, connect with industry leaders, and discover the people, places, and experiences shaping the future of African celebrations.

We’ll be bringing you along for the journey, sharing highlights from the conference, destination experiences, and the memorable moments that make Africa such a special place to celebrate.

Stay connected with us on BellaNaija’s social media pages and follow the conversation using #ADCCE2026, #UnveilingDestinationAfrica, #BNTravels.

Uganda, we’ll see you soon!

item.content:encoded:
The Leo Stan Ekeh Foundation (LSEF) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Nigeria Computer Society (NCS) to provide mentorship, technical training and real-world technology experience to the Nigerian whiz kids under the Foundation’s technology scholarship initiative.

The 1000 scholarship scheme, which was first announced by Africa’s foremost technology entrepreneur and Chairman of Zinox Group, Leo Stan Ekeh, is designed to empower indigent but exceptionally gifted Nigerian students to study Computer Science and other technology-related disciplines in federal and state universities, as well as polytechnics, across the country.

The scholarship reflects Dr. Ekeh’s philosophy of “one family, one tech-empowered person” and will support 1,000 students selected from all 36 states of the federation and the Federal Capital Territory, irrespective of ethnic background.

From their first year through graduation, beneficiaries will receive world-class technology training, skills development and monthly financial support. Each scholar will also have a dedicated mentor to provide guidance throughout their academic journey.

Under the MoU, the NCS will provide technical support and practical learning through experienced and certified technology professionals. The programme will blend academic learning with real-world exposure, helping beneficiaries build technical competence, problem-solving skills and the confidence to apply their knowledge beyond the classroom.

According to the Director of LSEF, Dr. George Emetuche, the programme will feature boot camps each semester, creating opportunities for students to learn beyond the classroom and gain practical experience. The objective, he explained, is to prepare beneficiaries not merely to graduate, but to become capable technology professionals who can solve real-world problems.

Speaking at the ceremony, NCS President, Professor Muhammed Siraju Aliyu, described Dr. Leo Stan Ekeh as a nationalist who has consistently supported initiatives that create opportunities for Nigerians who may otherwise lack access.

He noted that Dr. Ekeh’s relationship with the NCS predates the scholarship initiative and has contributed to the advancement of technology and human capital development. He also highlighted Dr. Ekeh’s technology innovation programmes, which identify young people with ideas, support them in developing their concepts and create opportunities for them to pitch to potential investors.

Professor Aliyu expressed appreciation for Dr. Ekeh’s contributions to the NCS and reaffirmed the Society’s commitment to initiatives that support national growth and development.

Representing the Zinox Group, Executive Director, Human Resources, Mrs. Chioma Nwoke, assured the Foundation and the NCS of the Group’s continued support for the initiative, cohort after cohort.

Beyond the scholarship, the programme represents a long-term investment in Nigeria’s human capital. By helping 1,000 gifted young Nigerians gain access to quality education, technology skills, mentorship and practical experience, the initiative can contribute to a stronger pipeline of home-grown technology professionals, innovators and problem-solvers.

item.title: Watch Asake Trade Big Scenes for Studio Sessions in His “Oba” Music Video
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com

Asake has released the official music video for "Oba" from his M$NEY album, trading big-budget street scenes for an intimate studio session alongside producers and backing vocalists.

item.content:encoded:
Asake leans into his royal theme and signature high-steeze style, reflecting the confidence behind his hit track Oba. Photo Credit: Mr Money/Instagram

Asake is keeping his foot firmly on the pedal, delivering fresh visuals for “Oba” from his latest project M$NEY. Directed by Director Buise, the newly released music video moves away from typical high-energy street setups to take fans directly inside the intimate, creative atmosphere of a late-night recording session.

At its core, “Oba”—which translates to King in Yoruba—is a high-steeze anthem centred on royal status, relentless hustle, and staying grounded. Across the track, Asake leans into his “Mister Money” persona, blending Yoruba cultural references with reflections on his unstoppable work ethic. He balances bragging rights about his dominant position in the industry with street wisdom and gratitude, reminding listeners to remain vigilant and humble even as international success rolls in.

On set for his Oba music video, Asake highlights his signature high-steeze look with a textured jacket and luxury travel accessories. Photo Credit: Mr Money/Instagram

The visual brings this context to life, opening with a bass player laying down a rhythmic groove in a dimly lit studio before panning to Asake seated in the vocal booth. Clad in a green tracksuit over a white tank top, accessorised with thick gold chains, rings, and sunglasses, the YBNL star records his lines while surrounded by producers, engineers, and backing vocalists. The clip blends performance shots with real-time studio mechanics, showing engineers fine-tuning mixing boards, vocalists harmonising at the microphone, and producers triggering beats.

Produced by long-time collaborator Magicsticks, “Oba” combines Asake’s signature log-drum rhythms with choir-backed harmonies. Rather than relying on large dance ensembles or cinematic storylines, the visual focuses on the pure craftsmanship behind the music, giving audiences a fly-on-the-wall perspective of how the hit came together in the studio.

item.title: Permission to Call Nancy Isime Madam EP? The Actress Is Making Her Executive Producer Debut!
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Nollywood star Nancy Isime has announced her debut as an executive producer, stepping behind the camera to lead her first film project and share the journey behind the scenes.

The post Permission to Call Nancy Isime Madam EP? The Actress Is Making Her Executive Producer Debut! appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Nancy Isime steps into her new role as an executive producer wearing a metallic brown ensemble paired with a gold statement necklace.

Permission to call Nancy Isime Madam EP? Because the Nollywood star has just announced that she is stepping into a new role, and this time, she will be calling some of the shots behind the camera. Nancy is making her debut as an executive producer, taking on a new side of filmmaking after years of entertaining us on screen.

You know her from films and series such as Blood Sisters, Shanty Town, Kambili: The Whole 30 Yards, Superstar and Obama‘M. Now, Nancy wants us to follow her as she takes on the business of making a film, from the early meetings to sponsorship discussions and marketing. And she is letting us in on the process from the very beginning.

In the video announcing the news, Nancy wore a brown outfit with an oversized collar, structured shoulders and gathered balloon sleeves. She paired it with a gold leaf statement necklace and finger-wave hair, looking ready for the boardroom before getting into the business of filmmaking. But beyond the outfit, it was what she had to say that got us listening.

Nancy Isime marks her transition behind the camera as an executive producer in a custom metallic brown dress with a flounced hem.

“Well yes, you’ve known me as an actor. But this time, I’m stepping into a completely new chapter. This is my first production as executive producer!”

And while she is excited about the new role, Nancy is not pretending she has everything figured out. She admitted that taking this step comes with a few nerves, saying, “Oh my God, guys, I can’t lie… I’ve never… my heart is doing gbi-gbi-gbi-gbi-gbi. Can I do this? Can I do this? Am I ready? I think it’s about time. Me self don try, huh?”

We love that she is bringing us along for the ride, because Nancy is not keeping this experience behind closed doors. She wants her audience to see what goes into getting a film made, including the meetings, sponsorship conversations and marketing decisions that happen long before a project reaches our screens.

Official actor profile image of Nigerian actress and TV presenter Nancy Isime, known for starring roles in Blood Sisters, Shanty Town, and Superstar. Photo Credit: Nancy Isime/Instagram 

“But I need you guys. I really, truly need you,” she said. “So come with me on this journey. Let’s go behind the scenes. Let’s go to the meetings, the sponsorship… Let’s do some marketing… We’ll see how it goes, guys. So see what I do. But for now, I’m just really excited to announce this to you. So, let’s begin. Shall we?”

The announcement also comes with glimpses of Nancy stepping out for corporate engagements, attending meetings, getting styled on set and speaking with camera operators. It looks like we will be seeing a lot more of what happens on the production side, rather than only the finished work on screen.

item.dc:creator: Wunmi Adelusi
item.description:
How do you balance it? That is one of the first questions women ask when they meet another woman who seems to have it all: the career, the family, the side projects, the composure. I understand the question. I’ve asked it myself. But the longer I live, the more convinced I am that we are asking […]

item.content:encoded:
A confident, stylish woman descends city stairs, embodying elegance and modern business fashion. Photo Credit: Ono Kosuki/Pexels

How do you balance it?

That is one of the first questions women ask when they meet another woman who seems to have it all: the career, the family, the side projects, the composure. I understand the question. I’ve asked it myself. But the longer I live, the more convinced I am that we are asking for something that does not exist.

When we ask for balance, we are really asking for the two sides of the scale to weigh the same, all the time. Equal weight to work and home. Equal weight to ambition and rest. Equal weight to the people who need the self and us we are trying not to lose. A scale, perfectly level, held steady every single day.

But nothing honest works that way.

Consider this: every major system of thought humanity has ever built carries a trade-off; a cost baked into its benefit. Prioritise individual freedom, and you risk the collective; protect the collective, and you constrain the individual. There has never been a framework, political or economic or moral, that delivered every good thing at once with no side effect. That is why no government pleases all its people, and why even the most admired ideas have always had their critics. If perfect balance cannot be engineered into our grandest theories, why do we expect to achieve it in a single human life, lived in real time, with finite hours?

Balance, I’ve come to believe, is a myth. Not a lie exactly, but a mirage. You cannot give one hundred per cent to everything simultaneously. Something always gives. The only real question is whether you are choosing what gives, or letting it be chosen for you.

So I’ve stopped chasing balance. I’ve started practising seasons.

In every season of life, the demands are weighted differently. There are seasons when work must take more. Seasons when family must. Seasons of building, and seasons of recovering. The wisdom is not in holding all things equal; it is in reading accurately which season you are in, and letting your energy follow it without guilt.

Within each season, there is a second discipline, one borrowed from an analogy many will know: learning to tell your glass balls from your rubber ones. Some of the things we juggle are rubber. If you drop them, they bounce. The deadline that can shift. The event you can miss. The email that can wait till Monday. They feel urgent, but they recover.

Others are glass. Drop them, and they crack, sometimes beyond repair. Your health. A child’s childhood. A marriage. Your integrity. Certain relationships and certain moments that do not come round again. The tragedy is how often we exhaust ourselves protecting the rubber balls, answering every message, meeting every expectation, saying yes to everything, while a glass ball slips from the other hand.

Knowing the difference is the real skill. Not balance. Triage. So when someone asks me how I balance it all, my honest answer is: I don’t. Nobody does. What I try to do instead is stay awake to my season, and clear-eyed about which balls in my hands are glass.

Some days I get it right. Some days a glass ball wobbles and I catch it just in time. Some days I let a rubber one fall on purpose, and feel the strange relief of choosing. That, I think, is the most any of us can do. Not a perfectly level scale, but a steady pair of hands, and the wisdom to know what must never be allowed to break.

Nigerian poet and lawyer Ogaga Ifowodo has won the 2026 Nigeria Prize for Literature, sponsored by Nigeria LNG Limited (NLNG), for his poetry collection, Why Does God Need a Gun?

Ifowodo’s win adds to a distinguished literary career spanning several decades. His other poetry collections include Homeland and Other Poems, which won the 1993 Association of Nigerian Authors (ANA) Poetry Prize; Madiba, which won the 2003 ANA/Cadbury Poetry Prize; The Oil Lamp, which won the 2005 ANA/Gabriel Okara Poetry Prize; and A Good Mourning, which was shortlisted for the Nigeria Prize for Literature in 2017.

The 2026 edition of the Nigeria Prize for Literature focused on poetry and attracted 223 submissions. Ifowodo’s winning collection emerged from a final shortlist that included James Ngwu Eze’s Unbind Me Now and Tares Oburumu’s Flora’s Love Colony.

NLNG’s Nigerian Prize for Literature is the biggest literary award on the continent, and the award comes with a $100,000 cash prize.

item.content:encoded:
Sometimes, when two artists find themselves together in a studio, they find it difficult to spark a connection. They can make a song together, but it might feel like climbing a cliff if they try to make another song. Meanwhile, some artists have that connection, that synergy, that whenever they find each other in the studio, they produce magic. They make beautiful, sweet music. For instance, Wizkid and Asake, who have not only featured one another on each other’s albums, Morayo and Lungu Boy, respectively, but have also released a joint project, an EP. As Wizkid puts it in their interview, they have had “successful collaborations.” There are artists like that who find creativity in the other’s creativity.

So are BNXN and FOLA, whose music, when carefully compared in terms of lyricism, could be considered the same. They do not sound the same; no, two artists can never sound the same, but you could always imagine BNXN on a FOLA, and vice versa. And they have shown their fans that whenever they find each other on a song, there is always a synergy. Actually, FOLA sang in “how many“, off his sophomore album, ‘9‘, “Mo Korin bi BNXN,” which means, I sing like BNXN.

The journey began with the remix of FOLA’s hit song, Alone, and BNXN was featured. The collaboration introduced listeners to what would become one of the more interesting musical partnerships in Nigerian Afrobeats. BNXN brought his familiar, soulful delivery to the song, complementing FOLA’s smooth vocals and emotional approach to music.

Then came Very Soon, a song on BNXN’s 2025 album, Captain, which featured FOLA. This time, FOLA joined BNXN on his own record, returning the favour and showing that their connection was not limited to one artist’s sound. They could find each other on either side of a collaboration and still make it work. Their musical relationship continued with Shamaya, another joint recording on BNXN’s Still in Charge EP.

Now, the two artists have reunited on my type, a song on FOLA’s sophomore album, 9, released on October 9, 2026. But for listeners who have followed BNXN and FOLA’s journey together, “My Type” is another opportunity to enjoy a pairing that has consistently found room for both artists to shine.

BNXN and FOLA have given their listeners reasons to always look forward to what they might create together next. If their collaborations so far are anything to go by, this is one musical partnership worth keeping an eye on. For now, fans will enjoy BNXN’s latest EP, Still in Charge and FOLA’s sophomore album: the 14-track project that features other notable Nigerian and African artists, including Davido, Ayra Starr, Darkoo, Bella Shmurda and Zlatan.

It is also about staying active, moving more and making healthier choices every day. As we celebrate World Heart Day and a decade of WalkHeartOn, we are proud to have created a platform that brings Nigerians together to take meaningful steps towards healthier hearts.”

For many attendees, it was a chance to exercise with friends and family. For others, it was an opportunity to meet new people, enjoy performances and simply step away from the usual routine. item.title: Women Innovators Building Smarter Ways to Live, Eat and Stay Healthy in Africa
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com

By Bayer Foundation and Impact Hub

The post Women Innovators Building Smarter Ways to Live, Eat and Stay Healthy in Africa appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Across Africa, some of the most interesting solutions to everyday problems are being built by women who have experienced those problems up close.

A doctor sees patients struggling to access cardiac screening and builds an AI-powered ECG device. A nurse watches patients lose hours navigating the healthcare system and creates a digital platform to make it easier. A food entrepreneur sees farmers lose the value of their harvest and builds the processing infrastructure they need.

An agronomist looks at Morocco’s water crisis and asks a different question: what if we could grow more food with far less water? These are the stories behind five of the 15 women named as 2026 Bayer Foundation Women Entrepreneurs Award winners globally, powered by the Impact Hub Network.

The five African awardees come from Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria and Morocco, joining 10 other women entrepreneurs selected from across Latin America and Asia.

From Kenya and Ethiopia to Nigeria and Morocco, their businesses are rethinking how communities access healthcare, preserve food and adapt to a changing climate. Each will receive €25,000 in non-dilutive funding alongside a six-month accelerator designed to help them strengthen their businesses and take their solutions further.

Meet the women behind the ideas

Dr. Alice Muhuhu of Aurora Health Systems, Kenya

Alice started Aurora Health Systems after seeing patients arrive at the hospital with advanced heart conditions that could have been detected much earlier.

Her answer is an AI-powered, portable ECG device designed to work offline and in low-resource clinics. It can detect more than 50 cardiac conditions and is already being used across more than 100 clinics in Kenya. But Alice is also tackling another problem in healthcare: whose data gets represented. Less than 1% of global ECG data comes from African populations, so Aurora is building a large-scale African cardiology dataset to help develop technology that better reflects the people it is intended to serve.

Beamlak Alemayehu of Medanit Digital Health, Ethiopia

For Beamlak, the healthcare problem was not always whether treatment existed. Sometimes, it was simply finding it. The former clinical nurse and social worker founded Medanit after seeing patients travel long distances, wait hours, and move between hospitals and pharmacies just to find the right care.

Medanit brings those services together through an app, website, and low-bandwidth call centre, allowing people to connect with doctors, medication, and mental health services without requiring everyone to have the same level of internet access or digital literacy.

In 2025, the platform reached more than 58,000 users and onboarded over 500 doctors and 60 healthcare partners.

Funmilayo Ishola  of Dehydrator Hub, Nigeria

Funmilayo grew up watching her mother trade fresh produce in Lagos markets and saw how quickly food could lose its value when there was nowhere to process or preserve it. That experience inspired Dehydrator Hub, which gives small food businesses and farmers access to solar-powered dehydrators, packaging equipment and technical training without requiring them to buy the machinery themselves.

More than 75 tonnes of fruit and vegetables have already been processed through the model, while farmers using the service have recorded income increases of 30–35%. Funmilayo has also trained more than 3,000 women.

Her bigger vision is to establish 776 processing hubs across Nigeria, one for every local government area.

Sokayna Bellam of Jodoor Greentech, Morocco

For Sokayna, the future of food begins with a simple question: how do you keep farming when water is becoming harder to find? The agronomist founded Jodoor Greentech to explore that question through hydroponic farming. The company now operates 10 greenhouses across 3,500 square metres, producing around 100 tonnes of fresh produce annually.

The system uses up to 90% less water than conventional farming and eliminates chemical pesticides. For Morocco and other water-stressed regions, it offers a glimpse of what agriculture could look like when farmers have to produce more with considerably less.

Omowunmi Emmanuel-Ogah of ExCare Health, Nigeria

During the COVID-19 pandemic, pharmacist Omowunmi encountered a mother who rushed into her pharmacy with her sick four-year-old son because she had nowhere else to turn.

The experience made her think differently about what a community pharmacy could be. Today, ExCare Health combines pharmacy services with diagnostics, vaccination and primary care. It operates five pharmacies, two diagnostic laboratories and an accredited immunisation centre across Lagos and Ogun State. Through its Vaxreach programme, ExCare has also helped turn eight pharmacies across five states into vaccination hubs.

Omowunmi’s ambition is to show what could happen if Nigeria’s thousands of community pharmacies became part of the country’s primary healthcare infrastructure. Supporting women to take good ideas further.

What connects these five women is not simply that they are working in technology, healthcare, or agriculture. It is that their businesses started with problems they could see around them.

The Bayer Foundation Women Entrepreneurs Award is designed to help founders like these move from solving a local problem to reaching more people. Since 2021, the Bayer Foundation has supported women-led enterprises in health and food security through non-dilutive funding, networks and structured support for growth.

Through its partnership with the Impact Hub Network, the programme adds local entrepreneurial networks, mentorship and access to a wider community of impact-driven founders.

For the 2026 awardees, the next chapter is about scale: taking solutions that are already working and figuring out how far they can go.

As BellaNaija turned 20 this year, we reinforced one important thing: strengthening the core the platform started with. BN was launched to showcase Africa’s beauty to the world through stories, fashion and weddings. To deepen this commitment, everything we have done this year reinforces the platform’s foundations. From the recent Grand Red Carpet Experience, tagged High Fashion Icon, which is an avenue to celebrate Africa’s vibrant culture, to On Our Radar, a series I launched in August to spotlight a few Nigerian artists whose distinct voices are projected to define Afrobeats in the future.

Through August and September, four artists were spotlighted, each sharing what inspired them to start making music and their absolute dream with music. The series was launched to further strengthen what BellaNaija is known for, which is showcasing African creatives to the world, even before they become global.

The spotlights are as follows:

Solana

For Solana, music has always been a natural way to express herself. She began writing songs at six and took her first steps towards making music professionally while at university, after her roommate introduced her to a recording studio. She describes her sound as YoruPop, an experimental blend that allows her to explore different sounds, emotions, and ideas without being confined to one genre. Her ultimate dream is to share African culture with the world through music that remains authentic to her roots, inspires people to embrace who they are, and leaves a lasting cultural impact.

Read her feature here.

Firstklaz

Firstklaz grew up surrounded by music, but it was seeing people connect with his songs, sing his lyrics back to him, and relate to his stories that convinced him to pursue it as a career. His sound blends African rhythms and Hausa culture with modern Afrobeats production, bringing together traditional melodies, storytelling, and contemporary influences. Beyond chart success and awards, his dream is to reach a global audience, sell out concerts around the world, create music that people will return to for decades, and inspire a new generation of African artists to embrace their cultural identities.

Read his feature here.

Abefe

Music has been a part of Abefe’s life since childhood, and his passion for singing eventually found a wider audience through his TikTok covers and relatable, vulnerable storytelling. His songs offer listeners a glimpse into his thoughts, experiences, and perspectives on life, allowing them to connect with the person behind the music. For Abefe, success means being able to shut down London’s O2 Arena with ease — a bold ambition that reflects his desire to grow from an emerging artist into a major name on the global music scene.

Read his feature here.

KW33N B

KW33N B, also known as B3NEDICTA, grew up surrounded by music, but discovering that she could create her own songs from her thoughts, emotions, and experiences made her see music as more than a passion. It became an outlet for self-expression and a place where she felt understood. Her sound blends Afrobeats, soul, and pop, drawing inspiration from everyday life and the human experience. Her ultimate dream is to share her music with the world, connect with people across cultures, and create timeless songs that bring listeners happiness, comfort, and a sense of connection long after their release.

Read her feature here.

At the heart of the experience was Glenfiddich’s belief that exceptional craftsmanship is found in the details. This philosophy also defines the brand’s partnership with the Aston Martin Formula One Team, connecting the worlds of whisky and engineering through a shared appreciation for precision, curiosity and attention to detail. The post BN Prose: Is Grammar Still a Legal Tender in This Country? By Toyosi Onikosi appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
A young man rests on a stack of books at a desk, sunlight filtering through a window. Photo Credit: Oladimeji Ajegbile/Pexels.

They buried Ebiakpo’s father, Papa, in June. The rain that day was the small, annoying kind that did not commit. Papa had taught History for thirty-one years. When he died, the state owed him nineteen months of salary and a pension nobody could prove existed. Ebiakpo was the third of four children, and the scholar. That was his role. His father’s small revenge on a country that had refused to pay him: he would build one more of himself, and this one would be paid what he was owed. Ebiakpo read Law. First class.

In August, he went for an interview at a firm on Victoria Island. The partner who saw him spent twenty minutes bragging about representing a luxury influencer accused of beating two girlfriends and turning up at his own arraignment high. The firm offered Ebiakpo 130,000 naira a month. Transport alone would have eaten seventy. On the bus home, he did the arithmetic and understood, for the first time, that his father had not died of a stroke.

His eldest brother Tamunotonye did the thing they did not name. He now called himself Chief Dollar Papi Money and had it airbrushed onto the boot of the BMW X6 he parked sideways at family functions. His large diamond chain hung to his navel. His girlfriend, Blessed, came with him everywhere, in a waist-length lace-front, acrylics she could barely type with, and a BBL he paid doctors in Turkey to install, as rumours had it. The chain around her neck hung a huge pendant that spelt Quila B — half for tequila, which was the only thing she drank, and half for the American popstar she was studying to become.

Chief Dollar took Ebiakpo to a place on the island where the drinks cost more than Ebiakpo’s rent. “Bro”, he said, wiping his mouth, “survival for this country no be grammar again. Na money. Na feeding your people. School na the biggest client Nigeria don ever run”. At the next table, a boy was livestreaming and shouting at his own phone. When the waitress bent to ask him softly to lower his voice, he turned and told her, at full volume, that a girl her size should be grateful he was patronising the restaurant she cleaned. His table applauded.

The second brother, Preye, had broken Papa’s heart. He read Engineering at the University of Portharcout but left in his third year to do music. He did not do music. He managed a boy from the streets called Flexable, who could not finish a sentence in any language. Flexable’s last single had crossed five million streams in a week. Preye carried Flexable’s water bottle and towels to shows and said he was investing in the brand. Papa never once asked him about the music.

Before he died, Papa said one afternoon in the parlour, while watching TV. “This country no longer celebrates excellence. It now rewards performed foolishness, because foolishness travels faster on the internet than sense.”

Ebiakpo’s sister, Papa’s only daughter, Tarilaye, was fifteen. She did not know the capital of Taraba. When he told her Jalingo, she said no; she was sure Jalingo was a dance, then thought about it and said sorry, that one was Alingo, and laughed at herself for a whole minute. Her plan, she had told their mother, was to become an influencer first, then a reality-show girl, then to marry a musician, or possibly an actor; she was still deciding.

Tarilaye had been the brilliant one. Before Papa died, she had read all Chinua Achebe cover to cover at eleven and even corrected her teachers in school. But school na scam had become a hymn in her generation, and she quietly stopped trying. She turned instead to endless scrolling and devotion to the lives of celebrities who did not know her name. She was happier now, or something that looked from a distance like happier.

The Yoruba word for one who knows zero used to be the worst thing a boy could call another in a schoolyard — Olodo. Now the ones who know zero owned everything the market would price. Ebiakpo’s first-class certificate lived in a drawer. It smelled faintly of batteries. One night, Ebiakpo had dreamt his father was still teaching. The classroom was empty. He was writing on the board in his beautiful handwriting, and behind him, through the window, the whole country was dancing.

He woke, and started thinking about which of his father’s children was the actual dullard.

item.content:encoded:
For a growing number of Nigerian businesses, Canada is no longer just where family lives or where people go to study. It is a market.

Businesses in Lagos pay Canadian software vendors, consultants, logistics partners, and collaborators. But for many, the payment is still the hardest part of the relationship. Transfers sit in “processing” for days. Exchange rates shift before the money lands. Recipients ask, politely at first, whether anything has been sent.

Oneremit, the cross-border payments platform built for African businesses, is closing that gap, with payments to Canada settling in minutes.

The approach starts with regulation. Oneremit is registered with FINTRAC, Canada’s financial intelligence agency, and complies with the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) under the supervision of the Bank of Canada. That foundation allows payments to reach Canadian recipients through [local rails such as Interac and EFT], the same networks Canadians use every day, rather than long correspondent banking chains.

For the business sending the money, the effect is simple: paying a partner in Toronto starts to feel like paying one next door.

The same infrastructure powers Nexus by Oneremit, the company’s education payments platform, helping Nigerian families pay tuition to Canadian universities before deadlines, not after them.

“Businesses in Lagos, Accra and Nairobi are doing business with the world, and they deserve infrastructure that treats them that way,” says Hammed Afenifere, CEO and co-founder of Oneremit. “That is the standard we are building to,” He added.

According to Chibuzor Uchenwoke, Oneremit’s Head of Marketing, businesses want less features and more certainty.

“They want to know when a payment leaves, when it lands and exactly what their recipient receives. Getting the regulatory foundation right in Canada is what makes that possible.” Chibuzor said.

The Canada corridor is one part of a wider regulated network. Oneremit holds IMTO licensing in Nigeria and Money Services Business registration with FinCEN in the United States, with expansion underway in the United Kingdom and Ghana. Today, the platform helps African businesses pay and get paid across more than 100 countries.

Lagos and Toronto are roughly 9,000 kilometres apart. For the businesses moving money between them, that distance is finally starting to feel smaller.

Businesses can get started at Oneremit.co.

item.title: Nigerian Engineer Yinka Ogunbiyi’s HaloBraid Wins $75,000 Harvard Innovation Prize
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Nigerian-born Harvard alum Yinka Ogunbiyi won the $75,000 grand prize at the 2025 Harvard President's Innovation Challenge with HaloBraid, an automated braid-assist device engineered to complete braids up to five times faster.

The post Nigerian Engineer Yinka Ogunbiyi’s HaloBraid Wins $75,000 Harvard Innovation Prize appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Harvard graduate Yinka Ogunbiyi, creator of the automated HaloBraid device engineered to complete braids up to five times faster. Photo Credit: Yinka Ogunbiyi/Instagram

Nigerian-born engineer and Harvard graduate Yinka Ogunbiyi has taken the technology and beauty worlds by storm with HaloBraid, an automated braid-assist device designed to complete hand-started braids up to five times faster. Created alongside her co-founder, David Afolabi, HaloBraid recently won top honours and the $75,000 grand prize in the Alumni & Affiliates Open track at the 2025 Harvard President’s Innovation Challenge. Designed to support high-impact ventures emerging from Harvard’s global network, the annual competition celebrates ground-breaking solutions to real-world challenges. HaloBraid slashes traditional styling times from hours to minutes, reducing physical strain like carpal tunnel and back pain for braiders while allowing salons to comfortably double their daily clients.

The idea for HaloBraid came directly from Ogunbiyi’s personal experience as a braid enthusiast. During the COVID-19 lockdown, the Harvard-trained engineer spent four long days trying to install her own knotless braids. That tedious experience sparked a lightbulb moment: building smart engineering to handle the repetitive, time-consuming part of hair braiding while keeping the stylist completely in control of the craft.

The official design of HaloBraid, the world’s first automated braid-assist device launching commercially in autumn 2026. Photo Credit: Yinka Ogunbiyi/Instagram

Now backed by over $7 million in funding and with more than 7,000 salons eagerly sitting on its waiting list, HaloBraid is gearing up for its official commercial rollout. Adding even more creative authority to the vision, world-renowned celebrity hairstylist Vernon François has officially joined the team as Creative Engineer. Reflecting on his role in shaping this next-generation beauty technology, François shared:

I am proud to announce that I have joined Halo as a Creative Engineer. This milestone is the result of unwavering consistency, relentless curiosity, and the understanding that artistry is a form of intelligence. Decades of experience working with hair, people, and potential now empower me to shape the future. There is a significant difference between being invited to the room and searching for a seat at the table—and walking in to find your place already recognised. But this goes even further.

I haven’t been invited just to sit at the table. I’ve been invited to question its structure, influence its design, and define who it serves next. My perspective is an essential part of the process, not an addition. This is true meaningful collaboration. I am exactly where I am supposed to be. Not by coincidence, but through consistency, artistry, and a steadfast conviction that the knowledge we hold belongs in shaping the future. HaloBraid supports professional stylists by completing hand-started braids up to five times faster while matching their technique. Thank you to the Halo team for recognizing not only my work but the potential of what we will create together. The Art of Afro Hair isn’t standing outside the future asking to be included—it’s helping to engineer it.

The groundbreaking device is officially set to make its commercial debut in autumn 2026, launching first across select professional salons.

item.title: Zimbabwean Writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza Wins the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing for ‘The Blue Fighter’
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza has won the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, taking home the £10,000 award for his short story 'The Blue Fighter' published in The Shallow Tales Review.

The post Zimbabwean Writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza Wins the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing for ‘The Blue Fighter’ appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza, winner of the £10,000 Caine Prize for African Writing 2026. Photo Credit: Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza/Instagram 

African literature has a major reason to celebrate as Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza takes home the prestigious 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing. Announced for his remarkable short story ‘The Blue Fighter’, originally published in 2025 by The Shallow Tales Review, Kundizeza secures the £10,000 award after emerging from an exceptional 2026 shortlist. Often dubbed Africa’s premier short story distinction, the Caine Prize for African Writing annually honours outstanding African literary voices, bringing worldwide visibility to compelling creative narratives across the continent.

Based in Harare, Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza is a Zimbabwean novelist, thriller writer, and Associate Editor at African Writer Magazine. Before claiming the 2026 Caine Prize, Kundizeza earned recognition across the literary world, notably winning the 2024 Island Prize for Debut African Fiction for his novel manuscript Freelance, participating in the 2025 LOATAD Black Atlantic Residency, and earning a finalist spot in the 2018 Africa Book Club Short Story Competition. His triumph with ‘The Blue Fighter’ cements his place among contemporary African literary greats.

The winning story ‘The Blue Fighter’ offers a deeply moving exploration of family dynamics, sacrifice, and survival under tough conditions. The narrative follows Tinashe, a young boy whose family falls into financial hardship after his father leaves his profession to pursue his passion for building fish tanks. As money becomes increasingly scarce, Tinashe’s mother is forced to choose between her family’s survival and her husband’s dream. Examining fatherhood, ambition, and financial hardship, ‘The Blue Fighter’ examines the complicated ways in which family circumstances can shape the people within them.

To claim the prize, Kundizeza stood out among a talented group of five shortlisted writers from across the continent. The 2026 Caine Prize shortlist also featured Kenyan author Gladwell Pamba for ‘The Last Shop’ (published by Jahazi Press), Cameroonian writer Melara Mvogdobo for ‘Dieu Merci!’ (published by Literatur.Review), Nigerian writer and critic Akinwande Jordan for ‘So Long Now It’s Starting To Look Like Eternity’ (published by Naira Books), and Egyptian author and translator Yasmine Zohdi for ‘The Absence of Stains’ (published by The Republic).

Official shortlist for the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, featuring authors from Kenya, Egypt, Nigeria, Cameroon, and Zimbabwe. Photo Credit: Caine Prize/Instagram 

The 2026 judging panel, led by journalist Bola Mosuro, praised Kundizeza’s narrative for its emotional depth and technical precision. Speaking on the winning story, Chair of Judges Bola Mosuro said:

Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza draws readers in from the opening lines and never lets go. With luminous prose and characters who feel instantly familiar, this moving story explores denial, frustration, loyalty and quiet strength in a way that will resonate with people everywhere. Gripping, moving and beautifully crafted, Simbarashe captures the complexities of family, denial and devotion with remarkable emotional power. It’s a brilliant and unforgettable piece of storytelling told in a deceptively simple manner, but which has a profound and lasting impact.

Reflecting on what this monumental recognition means for his career and creative journey, Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza shared:

Winning the Caine Prize means a great deal to me. I’ve been writing for several years, often without knowing where the work would take me, just fitting it around everything else in my life. To have a story drawn from my own experiences recognised at this level makes all those everyday compromises feel worthwhile. Most of all, it gives me a little more belief that I can keep making room for this life as a writer.

item.content:encoded:
Temi Nkem stepping out in a royal blue mini dress paired with white pointed pumps for Day 1 of her BBNaija Season 11 media tour.

Temi Nkem in blue has us feeling blown away! Hey, don’t mind us, we’re trying to rhyme here, but have you seen how gorgeous Temi looks in this royal blue mini dress? Fresh from her BBNaija Season 11 win, the 21-year-old winner kicked off Day 1 of her media rounds in Lagos in a look that had colour, shape and one very fabulous fringe bag all working together.

The dress itself is the star of the show, with a fitted, body-skimming silhouette, a sharp V-neckline and those gorgeous long bishop sleeves. The sleeves bring plenty of volume to the mini dress, gathering neatly at the wrists before finishing with extended cuffs. Keeping the dress in one solid shade means the unusual sleeve shape gets to have its say without competing with prints or heavy embellishment.

Then there is the bag. Temi carried a matching royal blue envelope clutch covered in long, cascading fringe, which fell across her waist as she moved. It adds a completely different texture to the smooth dress and gives the look some movement without taking it in another colour direction. She stayed with the blue theme through her deep blue drop earrings, then brought in a thick gold cuff and stacked rings for contrast.

BBNaija 11 winner Temi Nkem’s beauty and accessory details, featuring a sleek low ponytail, smoky eye makeup, glossy nude lips, gold jewelry, and a matching royal blue fringe clutch bag.

And the shoes? A pair of white pointed-toe pumps that instantly changed the feel of the all-blue look. The bright white against the royal blue gives the outfit a clean finish, while her sleek centre-parted low ponytail, soft smoky eyes, defined brows and glossy nude lip keep the beauty look polished and let the dress remain the main attraction.

If you have been searching for how to wear a blue mini dress or wondering how to style a blue dress with white shoes, Temi’s look gives you plenty to work with. A strong colour does not need much competing with it, and her decision to keep the dress, bag and earrings within the same blue family shows how monochrome dressing can make one bold shade feel even more striking.

Temi Nkem shows how to hold a fringe clutch purse to add texture and movement to a monochrome royal blue dress.

The fringe clutch is another styling detail worth stealing for your own wardrobe. If your bag already has plenty of texture and movement, pairing it with a simple, solid-colour dress gives it room to stand out without making the whole outfit feel busy.

For her first day of media appearances as the new BBNaija Season 11 winner, Temi has certainly started on a stylish note. And if this royal blue look is anything to go by, we have a feeling her post-Biggie fashion diary is going to be a fun one to follow.

item.title: La Roche-Posay Announces Dates for Living Lab Nigeria in Lagos
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com

item.content:encoded:
La Roche-Posay has officially announced the dates for Living Lab Nigeria, its first Living Lab experience in the country and Nigeria’s first live skin science experience.

The experience will open to the public on 5 and 6 November 2026 at Oasis by The Five Palm, Victoria Island, Lagos, bringing together dermatological science, innovation, and expert-led skin education in an interactive setting.

Inspired by La Roche-Posay’s Living Lab in Paris, the Nigerian edition has been designed to bring people closer to the science behind their skin. Across two days, visitors will be able to explore some of the research, formulations, and innovations behind La Roche-Posay while learning more about concerns including hyperpigmentation, acne, sun exposure, sensitive skin, atopy, and skin barrier damage.

“Skincare has become an increasingly important conversation in Nigeria, but this interest needs to be matched by access to credible information,” said Nadia Amasa, L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty. “Living Lab gives us an opportunity to bring our science closer to the Nigerian people. Consumers can ask questions, engage with experts, and better understand their skin and the science behind La Roche-Posay products.”

A major part of the experience will be five dedicated Innovation Corners, each exploring the science and technology behind the Mela B3, Anthelios, Effaclar, Cicaplast, and Lipikar ranges.

Through demonstrations and interactive activities, visitors will be able to learn more about the relationship between UV exposure and pigmentation, what happens to acne-prone skin, the importance of the skin barrier, and how different skin concerns can be better understood and managed.

The experience will also feature the Blue House, taking guests through more than 50 years of La Roche-Posay’s dermatological research and innovation.

At the Scars of Life Cinema, visitors will be introduced to personal stories exploring the physical and emotional impact of skin conditions, with a focus on atopy, atopic-prone skin, and the role of Lipikar in its care.

For visitors with questions about their own skin, certified dermatologists and skincare experts will offer free consultations throughout the public experience, creating an opportunity to receive expert guidance and better understand individual skin concerns.

“Many people only see a dermatologist once a skin concern has become difficult to manage, and there is still a great deal of misinformation around concerns such as acne and hyperpigmentation,” said Dr. Folakemi Cole-Adeife, Consultant Physician & Dermatologist and member of the L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty MedSquad. “Creating spaces where people can engage directly with dermatologists and ask questions about their skin can support better understanding, earlier intervention, and more informed skincare choices.”

Visitors will also be able to shop their preferred La Roche-Posay products at the Living Lab Pop-Up Store, with 15% off purchases in partnership with Konga Health throughout the experience.

Event Details and How to Register

Living Lab Nigeria will first open on 4 November 2026 for dermatologists, pharmacists, and other healthcare professionals, alongside a media preview, ahead of the public experience on 5 and 6 November.

Registration for the public experience is free at www.livinglabnigeria.com. Visitors can select a time slot, which grants access to the full Living Lab experience.

For more information on Living Lab, visit www.livinglabnigeria.com or email lrp@livinglabnigeria.com.

About La Roche-Posay

Created by a pharmacist in 1975, La Roche-Posay is present in over 50 countries and is recommended by over 100,000 dermatologists worldwide. It provides a unique range of daily skincare developed for every skin type, from newborns to cancer patients, from UV protection to repairing severely fragilized skin. La Roche-Posay’s formulas are developed with exclusive selenium-rich thermal spring water, due to its antioxidant and soothing properties.

Developed using a strict formulation charter with a minimal number of ingredients at optimal concentrations, La Roche-Posay products undergo stringent clinical testing for efficacy and safety, even on sensitive skin. La Roche-Posay understands that skin health has a profound impact on overall wellbeing and works alongside the medical community to advance dermatology and pioneer new approaches to care. Committed to the skin we live in and the planet we live on. Since 2023, all products are manufactured in factories using 100% renewable energy.

item.content:encoded:
The Macallan joined Kokopelli Art Gallery in marking its fifth anniversary with a three-day celebration that brought together contemporary art, storytelling and craftsmanship, culminating in Epignosis I: Our Story First, an exhibition spotlighting the work of five emerging African artists from the inaugural Once Upon a Time (O.U.T) Residency.

Across the three days, from September 10 to 12, the gallery became a meeting point for artists, collectors, cultural tastemakers and creatives, with The Macallan adding a refined dimension to an experience centred on the value of time, craft and creative expression.

At the heart of the celebration was the O.U.T Residency, the first programme of the Kokopelli Art Foundation. The residency brought together five artists from Ethiopia, Ghana, Benin Republic and Nigeria, giving them two weeks to develop their practices through studio work, mentorship, research and creative exchange. The resulting works were presented as part of Epignosis I: Our Story First.

What made the exhibition particularly compelling was the distinct perspective each artist brought into the room.

Estifanos Solomon Gashaw, a painter and printmaker from Ethiopia, explores passion, conflict and personal narrative, often examining society’s responsibility towards vulnerable communities. His work considers the consequences of neglect and asks deeper questions about empathy, care and the kind of society being created for future generations.

Victor Chigozie Anachuna, a Nigerian contemporary painter based in Lagos, works primarily in realism, using figurative compositions to explore identity, power, social hierarchy and political instability. His practice examines how people navigate complex social structures, while challenging conventional ideas around Black identity and masculinity. His works have been exhibited in Nigeria and internationally, including Only Human at Curtiss Jacobs Gallery in New York.

From Ghana, Putin Bempong works across painting and installation, bringing folklore, environmental transformation and material experimentation into conversation. His process is deeply research-led, incorporating materials such as mining soil, contaminated water, resin and found objects. Through the recurring figure of Ananse, he examines themes of adaptation, survival, power and environmental exploitation.

Falhone Kemi Ogoun, from Benin Republic, works across drawing, painting and installation, exploring the space between appearance and essence. Drawing from her Yoruba and Nago heritage, her work often turns to the human face as a reflection of character, identity and inner beauty, creating a dialogue between cultural tradition and contemporary expression.

Completing the cohort, Vurzie Kimnaton, a photographer from Northern Nigeria, documents people, places, culture and everyday life through portrait and documentary photography. During the residency, she turned her attention to Lagos, observing its markets, neighbourhoods, bus stops and waterfronts and looking at familiar spaces through a fresh perspective.

Together, the works formed Epignosis I: Our Story First, a “Call and Response” exhibition that paired the five residency artists with a solo body of work by Ayoola Gbolahan. The format drew from African oral and musical traditions, placing two generations of artists in the same space and allowing their works to engage with one another.

For The Macallan, the experience reflected a natural connection between craftsmanship and creative practice. The brand’s presence complemented an exhibition where time, patience, process and attention to detail were central to the stories behind the works, creating a considered cultural experience without taking away from the artists at its centre.

The programme opened with a private dinner on September 10, followed by a private viewing on September 11 and the public opening on September 12. Epignosis I: Our Story First continues at Kokopelli Gallery in Ikoyi, Lagos, until November 8, 2026.

More than an anniversary celebration, the experience offered a glimpse into the evolving possibilities for African creativity, where art, heritage, craftsmanship and contemporary storytelling can exist in the same space. For the five O.U.T Residency artists, it marked the beginning of a new chapter as the founding OUTliers of the Kokopelli Art Foundation.

item.content:encoded:
I did not set out to become a designer. For most of my life, I was an environmental consultant, someone who thought in watersheds and impact assessments, who measured the footprint a project leaves on the land and on the people who live beside it. Fashion was not my plan. Belonging was not something I imagined I would ever have to design. Both found me anyway, on the road, in the middle of West Africa, in a length of hand-dyed cloth I could not stop looking at.

My name is Hajar Saaid. I was born in Rabat and raised in Morocco, in a culture where cloth is a language. In my family, as in so many Moroccan families, a kaftan is not simply bought and worn. It is made, adjusted, admired, and remade, passed between the hands of women who know how to turn fabric into an occasion. I grew up understanding that what you wear can carry your history in its seams. I just did not know, then, that I would one day spend my life listening to that idea.

Work is what carried me across the continent. I trained and built my career in sustainability, mostly around water, though anyone who works in the environment quickly learns that you are really working with everything: power, transport, roads, and above all, people. An Australian firm I worked with in Rabat asked whether I would move to West Africa. I said yes. That single yes became almost ten years in Ghana, and a decade of travelling for projects through Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Burkina Faso, and beyond.

Everywhere I went, I looked at the land, and I looked at the fabric. My training had taught me to ask what a project gives to a community and what it takes away, and I found I could not switch that question off in a market stall any more than on a job site. I saw textiles made entirely by hand, dyed in patterns that held generations of knowledge, and I wondered why so few of them ever travelled beyond the borders of the country that made them.

The turning point, what we call in French the declic, happened in Nigeria in 2022. I found a fabric so beautiful I could not leave it behind. I brought it home and made a few pieces, first for myself, then for my mother and my sisters. I was not thinking about a business. I was thinking about how the cloth felt, and how it seemed to belong to both of the places I called home. But people kept asking where the pieces came from.

So I began, the way I begin everything, by studying it from the inside. I did not wait to build a polished brand with a strategy already written. I made a small run of pieces and watched how people responded to them, in Ghana and in Morocco, at events where I was often the only one dressed the way I was dressed. What I saw was recognition. Women from West Africa, from Morocco, from Europe, from Asia, from America, all seemed to find something of themselves in the same garment.

The idea is what I call hybrid design. My work lives in the space where the geometry of Moroccan zellige, those interlocking tiles I grew up surrounded by, meets the colour and rhythm of West African Kente and hand-dyed batik. On one garment, two homelands share a single canvas and, somehow, agree. I did not invent either tradition. I only refused to choose between them, because I have never been asked to choose between them in my own life.

I named the brand Burdah. In Arabic, a burdah is a cloak or a mantle, and it is also the name of one of the most beloved poems in the Muslim world, a poem about a cloak given as an act of grace and healing. The word felt right to me. A cloak is the most human of garments. It wraps you, it protects you, it travels with you. For someone who left one home and built another, a cloak is not a metaphor I had to reach for. It is simply what I needed.

Because I come from the environmental world, I could not build this brand any other way than carefully. Everything is made by hand, in small runs, often only one or two pieces in a given colour. No factory, no mass production, no warehouse of unsold stock. I work directly with artisans and tailors in Ghana and in Morocco, and I keep the whole chain, from choosing the fabric and the dye to the final stitch, on this continent, by choice. I know it would be cheaper to make these clothes somewhere else, in greater quantity. That has never been the point. Even the offcuts stay with me, waiting to become something else, because waste was the first thing my old career taught me to see.

People sometimes ask whether it is strange to move from environmental consulting to fashion. To me, they are the same work in different clothing. Both are about what we leave behind. Both honour the hands and the places that make a thing possible. When a woman puts on one of my pieces, and I get to tell her where the fabric was dyed and who finished the hem, I watch something shift in her. She is not just wearing a dress. She is carrying a small, traceable piece of a long human story, and she becomes part of it.

I still travel between Rabat and Accra, between the country that raised me and the one that took me in. For a long time I thought I would have to belong to one or the other. Burdah is my answer to that. It is a cloak wide enough for two homes. And every time someone new puts it on, in a city I have never been to, I am reminded that culture was never meant to have borders. It was meant to be worn.

item.content:encoded:
Tiger Beer is bringing its partnership with Manchester United to life through the Uncage Party, a series of high-energy consumer experiences across Port Harcourt, Enugu, Aba, and Asaba. As Manchester United’s official beer partner, Tiger is taking its presence beyond traditional brand touchpoints and creating vibrant spaces where consumers can come together, have fun, and engage with the brand in a more immersive way. The experience will come to life in selected bars, giving guests the opportunity to enjoy an exciting mix of games, taste experiments, arts, street food, entertainment, giveaways, and other interactive activities.

At the heart of the experience is the idea of giving consumers a space to unleash their energy and Uncage their Tiger. Guests will be encouraged to take part in a variety of activities, test their skills, compete with friends, and challenge themselves, creating an atmosphere filled with movement, energy, and friendly competition. From face painting and interactive games to opportunities to win exciting prizes, the experience is designed to ensure there is always something happening and different ways for guests to get involved.

The Uncage Party also creates room for people to connect and enjoy the social side of spending time together. Whether through friendly competition, spontaneous conversations, shared laughter, or discovering something new, the experience is designed around the moments that naturally happen when people come together. Rather than simply providing a space to spend time, Tiger is creating an environment where consumers can participate, interact, and create memories with friends and other guests.

The experience further strengthens Tiger’s connection with Manchester United by translating the partnership into a consumer experience that feels relevant, energetic, and accessible. As the club’s official beer partner, Tiger continues to use its relationship with Manchester United as a platform to connect with consumers while bringing its own bold personality into the experience. The Uncage Experience provides another expression of that partnership, allowing consumers to engage with Tiger through entertainment, participation, and shared experiences.

Rolling out across Port Harcourt, Enugu, Aba, and Asaba, the Uncage Party reflects Tiger Beer’s ambition to create moments that are bold, social, and memorable. Each location will provide consumers with the opportunity to experience the brand in an energetic environment built around fun, participation, and discovery. Through these experiences, Tiger is inviting consumers to step out of the ordinary, embrace the moment, and Uncage their Tiger.

Follow Tiger Beer on Instagram @tigerbeerng for official updates and exclusive details on upcoming match day experiences.

item.content:encoded:
To celebrate four years of flying, ValueJet is giving back to the customers who have supported the airline since its first flight, with daily ticket giveaways and a Grand Prize that will take two winners to Accra or Banjul.

From 5 to 10 October 2026, four customers will be selected daily to win a complimentary ValueJet ticket.


From 5 to 31 October 2026, two Grand Prize winners will each win an all-expenses-paid getaway for themselves and a companion, with one winner travelling to Accra and the other to Banjul. Customers qualify by booking and travelling on ValueJet’s Boeing 737NG service to Abuja or Port Harcourt during the promotion period. Terms and conditions apply.

The promotion begins on the same day ValueJet’s first Boeing 737NG, registration 5N-CFZ, is scheduled to operate its first passenger flight from Lagos to Abuja on Monday 5 October. The aircraft is a significant fleet and product milestone for the airline and reflects its continued investment in the customer experience and its ambition to grow across West Africa.

“Four years ago, we set out to build an airline Nigerians could rely on,” said Omololu Majekodunmi, Managing Director of ValueJet.

“Reaching this anniversary alongside our first Boeing is a proud moment for our team, and it would not have been possible without the customers who have chosen to fly with us. Giving back through free tickets and a trip to Accra or Banjul is our way of saying thank you, and flying our first Boeing is our way of showing where we are going next.”

Throughout October, ValueJet will share winners’ stories and the experiences of long-standing customers on its social channels.

How To Take Part

  • Book a qualifying Boeing flight to Abuja or Port Harcourt at www.flyvaluejet.com.
  • Travel during the promotion period.
  • Qualifying customers are entered for the daily giveaway and the Grand Prize draw. Terms and conditions apply.

About ValueJet

ValueJet, operated by FlyForValue Aviation Ltd, is a Nigerian scheduled airline connecting major cities across Nigeria and West Africa. Founded in 2018, the airline commenced commercial operations in 2022.

From its hubs in Lagos and Abuja, it operates domestic services alongside regional flights to Accra, Banjul, Cotonou and Monrovia. ValueJet is expanding its fleet and network to strengthen connectivity across Nigeria and West Africa while providing safe, reliable and value-driven air transport.

For more information, visit www.flyvaluejet.com.
